cards.title: Polynomial-time minimum-total-length disjoint paths for fixed k
cards.formal: For every fixed integer k≥3, is there a polynomial-time algorithm that, given an undirected unweighted graph G and k prescribed terminal pairs (sᵢ,tᵢ), outputs pairwise vertex-disjoint paths Pᵢ from sᵢ to tᵢ minimizing ∑ᵢ|E(Pᵢ)|, or correctly reports that no such collection exists? Randomized algorithms with success probability at least 2/3 on every input are admitted in this reading, consistently with the randomized k=2 baseline cited by the source. Polynomial degree and constants may depend on k; an FPT bound with exponent independent of k is not requested.
cards.why: Would determine whether exact length optimization preserves the polynomial-time solvability of undirected disjoint routing with a fixed number of prescribed terminal pairs.
cards.status_note: Checked the original graph model and concluding question, the full 2025 cycle-packing discussion, and the exact scopes of the 2024 grid and 2025 planar results. Searches through 12 September 2026 identified no general fixed-k polynomial-time algorithm. Randomized bounded-error solvability is explicitly admitted as in the source’s k=2 comparison.

progress.text: The source improves fixed-k algorithms for individually shortest disjoint paths and leaves minimum-total-length routing open for k≥3.
Minimum-total-length routing is shown FPT in the special setting of an infinite rectangular grid.
The cycle-packing paper still lists the three-pair minimum-total-length routing problem as open, including on planar graphs.

references.title: Using a Geometric Lens to Find k Disjoint Shortest Paths
references.authors: Bentert, Matthias; Nichterlein, André; Renken, Malte; Zschoche, Philipp
references.locator: Unresolved-question passage on page 13; PDF page 13

cards.definitions: G is a finite simple connected undirected graph with n numbered vertices and unit length on every edge, encoded by an adjacency matrix and the terminal labels. Take the 2k terminals to be distinct; repeated endpoints across different pairs make vertex-disjointness infeasible, and a pair with sᵢ=tᵢ uses the zero-edge path at that vertex and can be handled separately. A path is a sequence of distinct vertices with consecutive vertices adjacent. Vertex-disjointness includes endpoints and means V(Pᵢ)∩V(Pⱼ)=∅ for i≠j. Pairings are fixed: connecting a source to a different pair’s target is not acceptable. Define OPT as the minimum sum of edge counts over all feasible collections and set OPT=∞ when there is none. The output consists of the k vertex sequences of an optimal collection, or an infeasibility answer. For each fixed k the algorithm is a probabilistic Turing machine, with one finite program handling all n and all inputs for that k, running in at most C_k(n+1)^{c_k} steps on every random-bit sequence. Constants C_k,c_k are independent of n. With probability at least 2/3 over its independent fair bits, the full output must be correct, including exact optimality. A deterministic algorithm is included as the zero-error case. The formulation asks for polynomial time for each fixed k and does not demand a uniform procedure generating these programs as k varies. The source compares this target with k-DSP, which requires every Pᵢ separately to have length dist_G(sᵢ,tᵢ). Such a collection, when it exists, has the smallest possible total length; minimum-total-length routing must also handle inputs where disjoint routes exist but no collection of individually shortest routes exists.
cards.answer_criterion: Establish or refute polynomial-time solvability, with the stated bounded-error allowance, for every fixed k≥3. A positive answer must output an exactly optimal collection or detect infeasibility on all inputs. A conditional negative answer must state its assumption and imply that no such polynomial-time algorithm exists for at least one fixed k. Hardness only when k grows with n, an FPT lower bound, approximation, or an algorithm restricted to individually shortest paths does not decide this question.

context_blocks.title: The objective permits necessary detours
context_blocks.text: Disjointness can force one route away from its own shortest path. The optimization problem allows such detours and asks for the smallest total number of edges over all routes. An algorithm checking only whether all individual shortest distances can be attained cannot handle the remaining instances.

context_blocks.title: Fixed k is the relevant complexity boundary
context_blocks.text: The source gives polynomial-time algorithms for individually shortest paths at every fixed k and cites a randomized polynomial-time algorithm for minimum total length when k=2. It leaves the minimum-total-length extension open for k≥3.

context_blocks.title: A specialized optimization result
context_blocks.text: The 2024 grid result handles minimum-total-length routing on an infinite rectangular grid. Its geometric restriction does not give the requested algorithm on arbitrary undirected graphs.

context_blocks.title: Planar shortest paths have a different objective
context_blocks.text: The 2025 planar preprint requires every route to be individually shortest. That condition does not handle general minimum-total-length routing when disjointness forces detours.

context_blocks.title: A recent source confirms the unresolved case
context_blocks.text: The published 2025 cycle-packing paper explicitly states that Min-Sum Disjoint Paths remains open even for three pairs on planar graphs. Its own polynomial-time result packs cycles without prescribed terminal pairs, so it does not settle this routing problem.

cards.title: Can StoqMA amplify both completeness and soundness?
cards.formal: For every pair of efficiently computable threshold functions a(n),b(n) with 1/2≤b(n)<a(n)≤1 and a(n)−b(n)≥1/q(n) for some polynomial q, and every integer-valued polynomial ℓ(n)≥2, is StoqMA(a,b) contained in StoqMA(1−2^{−ℓ(n)}, 1/2+2^{−ℓ(n)})? Here n is the classical input length. The new verifier must remain in the same one-witness stoquastic circuit model, with polynomially many gates, witness qubits and ancillas.
cards.why: Would determine whether the stoquastic verification model has ordinary exponential error reduction and, through the published equivalence, whether its proof power collapses to classical Merlin–Arthur verification.
cards.status_note: Read Conjecture 6, the verifier definition and soundness-only theorem, the 2025 published equivalence, and the relevant statements in the May and July 2026 preprints. No full one-witness amplification theorem was found through 12 September 2026. The July 2026 source explicitly still calls the general question open.

progress.text: Soundness-only error reduction is established, while Conjecture 6 states the simultaneous completeness/soundness target.
A published theorem establishes that general StoqMA error reduction is equivalent to StoqMA=MA.
A revised preprint on unentangled stoquastic proofs retains the general error-reduction problem as open and studies more restricted amplification guarantees.

sentences: A StoqMA verifier uses classical reversible gates, special initial ancillas and one final measurement in the plus/minus basis.
It accepts a suitable nonnegative quantum witness on yes instances and must reject arbitrary witnesses with the prescribed soundness bound on no instances.
The question asks whether every inverse-polynomial gap can be amplified to completeness exponentially close to one and soundness exponentially close to one half.
Soundness-only repetition is known, but it does not provide this simultaneous improvement.
A published theorem makes full error reduction equivalent to StoqMA=MA, and July 2026 work still states the general problem as open.

references.title: StoqMA Meets Distribution Testing
references.locator: Unresolved-question passage on page 6; PDF page 6

cards.definitions: A promise problem is a pair (L_yes,L_no) of disjoint sets of finite binary strings, with no required answer outside their union. Membership in StoqMA(a,b) means there is a deterministic polynomial-time procedure which, given x of length n, produces a verification circuit V_x on m(n)+r(n)+s(n) qubits, all counts polynomially bounded in n. Its initial state is |w⟩⊗|0⟩^{⊗r}⊗|+⟩^{⊗s}, where |+⟩=(|0⟩+|1⟩)/√2 and the m-qubit witness has norm one. The circuit uses only classical reversible gates: NOT flips a bit, CNOT flips its target if its control is one, and Toffoli flips its target if both controls are one. These gates act linearly on computational-basis states. There are no intermediate measurements or arbitrary quantum gates. At the end a designated output qubit is measured in the {|+⟩,|−⟩} basis, with |−⟩=(|0⟩−|1⟩)/√2, and outcome + means acceptance. Its acceptance probability is the squared norm after projection onto |+⟩ on that qubit. If x∈L_yes, some witness with real nonnegative computational-basis amplitudes must be accepted with probability at least a(n). If x∈L_no, every normalized witness, including arbitrary complex amplitudes, must be accepted with probability at most b(n). The source proves that a maximizing witness can be chosen nonnegative. Efficient threshold computability is understood in the standard precision sense: their values can be approximated within 2^{−t} in time polynomial in n+t. The inverse-polynomial gap permits this conventional representation. Class containment quantifies over promise problems and asserts existence of new uniform verifiers; it does not demand a blackbox compiler acting on an arbitrary verifier description. Polynomial bounds of the new verifier may depend on the original verifier, q and ℓ. Soundness approaches 1/2 from above, not zero; the requested improvement is relative to the stoquastic acceptance baseline.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the containment for every admissible a,b and ℓ, or refute this universally quantified amplification statement. A positive answer must achieve both exponentially small completeness error and exponentially small excess soundness above 1/2 while retaining the allowed gates, initial ancillas and final measurement. Soundness-only repetition, perfect-completeness special cases, extra destructive-interference gates, or additional unentangled provers do not establish the claim.

context_blocks.title: The verifier has a restricted way to accept
context_blocks.text: The computation is classically reversible, but its ancillas and final measurement allow a nonnegative quantum witness to affect acceptance. This restricted verification model arises in the complexity of stoquastic local Hamiltonians. Familiar error-reduction statements for unrestricted quantum verification do not automatically give the required stoquastic verifier.

context_blocks.title: Soundness reduction alone is known
context_blocks.text: The source’s Theorem 5 maps thresholds (1/2+u/2,1/2+v/2) to (1/2+u^r/2,1/2+v^r/2) for polynomial r. This improves excess soundness but can also lower completeness. Conjecture 6 asks for simultaneous amplification towards completeness one and soundness one half.

context_blocks.title: Amplification would identify StoqMA with MA
context_blocks.text: The 2025 published paper proves that negligible completeness error with a suitable inverse-polynomial gap is already contained in MA, the class of promise problems verified in polynomial time with a classical witness and random bits. Its Corollary 1.5 makes general StoqMA error reduction equivalent to StoqMA=MA.

context_blocks.title: Recent multiwitness work keeps the question open
context_blocks.text: The July 2026 preprint still explicitly calls general one-witness error reduction open. Its restricted repetition results do not supply the two threshold limits required here for arbitrary original completeness.

context_blocks.title: Prover collapse is a separate claim
context_blocks.text: The May 2026 preprint claims that the number of stoquastic provers can be reduced while retaining an inverse-polynomial gap. It explicitly avoids assuming general amplification. This preprint claim is not recorded as a solution of the one-witness error-reduction question.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
